caseno: Appeal from Appellate Decree No. 94 of 1965.
lawyer:
M.A. Mutalib---For the Appellant.
Kazi Ebadul Huq, for B N. Chowdhury---For Respondent No. 1.
parties:
Sukhendu Bikash De & anr  ----- Appellants.
Vs.
Nurul Islam & ors  ----- Respondents.
full_judgment:
The plaintiff appellant instituted a suit for redemption of the suit property mortgaged on 22-4-1924 during his minority by his sister's husband Prankrishna, as his guardian, to Abdur Rashid the predecessor of defendants 1 to 8. As the loan together with interest was satisfied out of the usufruct of the land enjoyed by defendants Nos. 1 to 8 the plaintiff demanded back the land, but was refused.

2. Defendants asserted that the lands were acute n purchased by defendant No. 9 in a rent suit with his money and for his own benefit and, while he was in possession defendant No. 8 purchased the same from him.

3. The trial court dismissed the suit and held that the plaintiff knew about the rent sale for a long time and he was estoppel by his own conduct from claiming redemption of the suit property. It was considered that as the rent suit related to arrear rent of a period prior to the mortgage the mortgagee was not responsible for the payment of that arrear rent, and the subsequent acquisition of the property by the heirs of mortgagee could not be held to be for the benefit of the mortgagor.

4. The lower appellate court affirmed the decree of the trial court. It considered that the sale certificate dated 15-12-25, Ext. B, showed that the balding relating to the Suit land was in arrear for rent for which the landlord brought Rent Suit No. 513 of 1924; that the rent suit must have been for arrear of rent due prior to April; 1924 that in the deed of the mortgage mortgagee did not undertake any obligation to pay arrear rents ; that there was no evince that defendant No. 9 was a benamdars of defendants 1 to 8; shat the name of the suction purchaser Hamid Ali Defendant No. 9, was recorded in the R.S. Khatian which prima facie proved his possession in the Suit land; that the R. S. Khatian, Ext. D and D(1) were prepared and finally published to the knowledge of the plaintiff or his guardian; that the plaintiff stated in the plaint that he was demanding the Suit land for the last 35 years, but in the court he reduced the period from 35 years to 16/17 years; that the defendants were claiming to be in possession in a different right other than one under the mortgage at least for 16/17 years; that they acquired an Indefeasible right against the plaintiff and the plaintiff's suit was time barred.

5. Mr. M.A. Muttalib, the learned Advocate for the appellant, has submitted that the mortgagee Abdur Rashid, in the absence of any contract to the contrary, having defaulted to pay the arrear rent accruing due in respect of the suit land during his possession and in default of such payment of arrear rent the suit land having been sold and the same having been purchased by his cousin defendant No. 9, and subsequently by his wife, defendant No. 8, the benefit accrued thereby will ensure to the mortgagor; that the admitted fact being that the relationship between the plaintiff and Abdur Rashid being that of mortgagor and mortgagee and the suit being governed by Article 148 of the Limitation Act, the mortgage and subsequent transfer having taken place within 60 years from the date of the mortgage the equity of redemption is available to the plaintiff-appellant; and that in view of the evidence and circumstances the mortgagee Abdur Rashid taking advantage of his fiduciary position all, wed the suit land to be sold for arrears of rent and same having been purchased in the names of his cousin and wife subsequently, the subsequent transferees are constructive trustee of the mortgagor and the plaintiff appellant is entitled to redeem the suit land.

6. Mr. Kazi Ebadul Huq, the learned Advocate for the respondent, has submitted that the lower appellate court found no evidence that defendant No. 9 was the benamdar of defendants 1 to 8 and that as the property, purchased by defendant No. 9 was recorded in his own name in R.S. khatian and it was long after transferred to defendant No. 8 that transfer did not or could not revive the plaintiff's right of redemption which had totally been extinguished by the rent sale. He has further contended that the mortgagee was not under any obligation to pay arrear rent for which the land could be sold in rent sale.

7. The deed of mortgage was executed on 29-4-24. Rent suit No. 513 of 1924 was disposed of on 22-12-24. The lower appellate court rightly held that the rent suit must have been for arrear of rent due prior to April, 1924. The deed of mortgage does not show that the mortgagee undertook the obligation to pay arrear rent.

8. Clause (c) of section 76 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, provides that a mortgagee will be under obligation in the absence of a contract to the contrary, to pay the Government revenue, all other charges of a public nature and all rent accruing due in respect of the mortgaged property during such possession and any arrear of rent in default of payment of which the property may be summarily sold.

9. In the present case the property was not summarily sold and as the rent was for a period prior to the mortgagee entered into the possession of the mortgaged property he was not under any obligation to pay arrear rent for which the land was not summarily sold, but sold in execution of a rent suit. In Jagat Mohan Nath Sahi Deo Vs. Sheonarsin Marwari and others, AIR 1938 Patna 197. It was held that the word 'summarily' occurring in the latter portion of section 76(c) of the Transfer of Property Act implied that the proceedings for realisation of rent by sale of the property were of a summary nature, for instance, as in the case of a certificate proceeding under the Public Demand Recovery Act. This view was later followed in Jay Prasad Choubey Vs. Mt. Jasoda and others, AIR 1958 Patna 649.

<u>10. In this case the mortgagor defaulted to pay the arrear rent and the mortgagee was not under any obligation either in law or in contract to pay the arrear rent for which the land was sold out in the execution of a rent decree and the right of redemption of the mortgagor was extinguished. In Gauri Shankar Sahu Vs. Sheotshal, AIR 1936 Patna 434, it was held that the rent sale extinguished the mortgagor's equity of redemption when it was not proved to be fraudulent. The same view was followed in Fekua Mahto Vs. Babu Lal Sahu, AIR Patna 382. In the present case the plaintiff's equity of redemption was extinguished for his own default to pay arrear rent and there is no evidence to show that the mortgaged property was collusively or fraudulently sold out for any default of the mortgagee.</u>

11. The next question that calls for determination in this case is whether defendants No. 1 to 8 can be held as constructive trustees under section 90 of the Trusts Act, 1882. Mr. Muttaleb has referred to the case of Jamila Khatun Choudhury Vs. Mahmud Khatun Choudhury, AIR 1918 Cal. 192. In that case the defendant, a mortgagee in possession of a share in a taluk, had undertaken to pay the Government revenue, but

made default in payment of the revenue, and the taluk was sold for arrears of revenues and was purchased by one Abdul Bari, who shortly afterwards sold it to the defendant, and the plaintiff, a purchaser from the mortgagor, sued to recover possession of the taluk from the defendant on Redemption, it was held that the sale for arrears of revenues and the subsequent sales to the defendant were collusive transactions engineered by the defendant for the purpose of obtaining possession of the taluk as owner this case has got no relevance in the case before me.

<u>12. In the present case the mortgagee or his heirs had not undertaken any obligation to pay arrear rent for which the land was sold in a rent sale and there was no evidence to show that the suit property was sold in the execution of a rent decree because of any default or any collusion of the mortgagee or their heirs Defendant No. 9 auction purchased the suit land on 15-12-25. His name was recorded in R.S. Khatian and, much later, on 14th Chaitra, 1290 M.E. corresponding to 2-4-1929 AD defendant No. 8 purchased the suit land from defendant No. 9. Mr. Ebadul Huq has referred to the case of Isar Nonia Vs. Karinam Panday, AIR 1958 Patna 353 and that of Jay Prosad Choubay vs. Mt Jasoda reported in the same, volume of the report at page 649 in support of his contention that section 90 of Trusts Act could only apply where the mortgagee in possession gained some advantage by availing himself of his position. Defendant No. 8 purchased the suit property from defendant No. 9 long after the equity of redemption in the mortgaged property was extinguished and hence, she or other heirs of Abdur Rashid could not be liable to hold the property for the benefit of mortgagor just because the subsequent transfer took place within the time prescribed for a suit of redemption of a mortgage. Had the mortgaged property been purchased by defendant No. 8 or had defendant No. 9 purchased the property in the benami of the heirs of Abdur Rashid or in collusion with them, then by operation of section 90 of the Trusts Act defendant Nos. 1 to 8 could be held responsible for holding the property for the benefit of the mortgagor and a fiduciary relationship between the mortgagor and mortgagee would have subsisted and the suit would have been within time under Article 148 of the Limitation Act. But as the facts are otherwise I must hold that the plaintiff's right of redemption was extinguished long ago when the mortgaged property was sold in execution of a rent decree.</u>

In view of the above, the appeal is dismissed with costs. Leave prayed for under clause 15 of the Letters Patent is refused.

End.
